## Why This Matters

In L05 the **Perceptron** looked like the end of a story: a clean linear classifier with a
convergence guarantee. Then, in 1969, Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert pointed out that it
**cannot even learn XOR** — a problem a child solves instantly — and the disappointment froze
neural-network research for over a decade.

The twist that restarted the entire field is almost anticlimactic: **stack the neurons**. One
neuron draws one straight line; a *layer* of neurons feeding a *second* layer can bend, fold,
and carve regions no single line can. Everything that followed — deep networks, convolutional
nets, transformers — is that one idea, scaled up. This lesson makes the move from *one neuron*
to *a network*, and pins down the single ingredient (a **nonlinear** activation) without which
the trick silently fails.

::: {.callout-tip title="Analogy"}
A single neuron is **one judge with one yes/no rule** — it can only split the world with a
straight cut. A network is a **small committee**: the second judge does not vote on the raw
evidence, but on *what the first judges concluded*. That extra level of indirection is what
lets the committee reach verdicts no single judge could. The catch — and the reason it took
until the 1980s — is that each judge's verdict must pass through a *nonlinear* step; otherwise
the committee is mathematically identical to a single judge.
:::

## From Perceptron to Neuron

The perceptron of L05 computed a weighted sum of its inputs and fired if the sum cleared a
threshold. Write that in two steps and you have the **artificial neuron** — the universal
building block of every neural network:

$$
z = w_1 x_1 + w_2 x_2 + \dots + w_n x_n + b = \mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{x} + b,
\qquad a = \phi(z).
$$

First a **linear** part (the same $\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b$ score you have seen since
L03), then a function $\phi$ — the **activation** — applied to it. The perceptron is exactly
this neuron with $\phi$ fixed to a hard *step*. The single new idea is that **$\phi$ is now a
free choice**, and that choice changes everything about what a network can do and how it is
trained.

::: {.callout-note title="A neuron is almost logistic regression"}
Set $\phi$ to the **sigmoid** and a single neuron *is* logistic regression (L04): score, then
squash to a probability. Set $\phi$ to a step and it is the perceptron (L05). The neuron is the
generalization that contains both — and, once stacked, far more.
:::

The model traces back to McCulloch and Pitts (1943), who showed that a network of absurdly
simple on/off units could compute any logical proposition, and to Rosenblatt (1958), who made
such a unit *learn* from data. We borrow the biology for intuition only: like an aircraft that
flies without flapping, artificial neurons long ago stopped resembling their biological cousins.

## Activation Functions

The activation $\phi$ is what makes a neuron more than a linear model. Four show up constantly:

| Activation | Formula | Range | Use it for |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Step / sign** | $\phi(z) = 1$ if $z \ge 0$ else $0$ | $\{0, 1\}$ | the perceptron; **not** trainable by gradient descent |
| **Sigmoid** | $\phi(z) = 1/(1 + e^{-z})$ | $(0, 1)$ | output layer for a probability (L04) |
| **Tanh** | $\phi(z) = \tanh(z)$ | $(-1, 1)$ | zero-centered hidden activation (classic) |
| **ReLU** | $\phi(z) = \max(0, z)$ | $[0, \infty)$ | **the modern default** for hidden layers |

The step function has a fatal flaw for learning: its slope is **zero everywhere** (and
undefined at 0), so gradient descent (L03) has nothing to follow — nudging a weight does not
change the output until it suddenly flips. The smooth activations fix this: sigmoid and tanh
have a usable slope, and **ReLU** — cheap to compute and with a constant slope of 1 for
positive inputs — has become the default hidden activation in deep networks. We will lean on
this in L16, where training *is* following those slopes.

## Layers

Stack several neurons side by side, each wired to **every** input, and you have a **dense**
(fully connected) layer. A perceptron is the simplest case: an **input layer** feeding a single
dense **output layer**. With linear algebra the whole layer is one expression,

$$
\mathbf{H} = \phi(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W} + \mathbf{b}),
$$

where $\mathbf{X}$ is one row per instance, $\mathbf{W}$ holds one column of weights per neuron,
$\mathbf{b}$ is the per-neuron bias (added to every row by broadcasting), and $\phi$ is applied
element-wise. This single matrix form is exactly what a GPU runs billions of times per second.

## The XOR Wall

Here is the wall. A single neuron computes one linear score, so its decision boundary is one
straight line (L04/L05) — it can only separate classes that a line can separate. **XOR** asks
for output 1 on $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ but 0 on $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$: the two positive corners sit
on *opposite* sides of the square, and **no single straight line** puts them together. In the
lab, a `Perceptron` fit to XOR scores **0.500** — pure chance — while the *same* model on the
linearly separable iris-setosa problem scores a perfect **1.000**. The failure is XOR's
geometry, not a bug in the code.

## Breaking the Wall with Depth

Add one **hidden layer** between input and output and the wall comes down. The trick is to have
the hidden neurons compute *intermediate* features, and the output neuron combine **those**:

- hidden neuron 1 = **OR** $(x_1, x_2)$
- hidden neuron 2 = **NAND** $(x_1, x_2)$ (not-and)
- output neuron = **AND** (hidden 1, hidden 2)

Because `XOR = (x1 OR x2) AND NOT(x1 AND x2)`, this two-layer network reproduces XOR exactly —
**1.000** in the lab, with weights we simply *wire by hand*. The output neuron never sees the
raw inputs; it sees what the hidden layer *concluded*, and on those derived features the
problem is linearly separable again.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  X1(("x1")) --> H1["hidden 1<br/>OR"]
  X2(("x2")) --> H1
  X1 --> H2["hidden 2<br/>NAND"]
  X2 --> H2
  H1 --> O["output<br/>AND -> XOR"]
  H2 --> O
```

::: {.callout-important title="The nonlinearity is the active ingredient"}
Depth alone is not enough — the activation must be **nonlinear**. A stack of purely *linear*
layers collapses: $\mathbf{W}_2(\mathbf{W}_1\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{W}_2\mathbf{W}_1)\mathbf{x}$
is just *one* linear map with a combined weight matrix, no more expressive than a single neuron.
The lab shows this directly — replace the hidden step with the identity and the XOR network
falls straight back to **0.500**. It is the nonlinear $\phi$, not the extra weights, that buys
depth its power.
:::

## What's Next — the Open Question

We *hand-wired* the XOR network's weights because we already knew the answer. Real networks have
thousands to billions of weights and must **learn** them from data. That raises the two
questions Unit V answers next:

- **How do you specify and run such a network in practice?** — **L15 (Multilayer Perceptrons)**,
  where we meet **PyTorch** and the universal-approximation idea.
- **How do you train all those weights by gradient descent?** — **L16 (Backpropagation)**, the
  algorithm that pushes the error backward through the layers.

## Common Pitfalls

- **"A single neuron is more powerful than logistic regression."** It is not — one neuron is
  still a single linear boundary. The power comes from *stacking* into hidden layers.
- **Wide but shallow.** Adding more neurons to *one* layer does not break the linear wall; you
  need at least one **hidden** layer between input and output.
- **Forgetting the nonlinearity.** Stacked *linear* layers collapse to a single linear layer —
  the depth is wasted. A nonlinear activation between layers is mandatory.
- **Training with a step activation.** The step has zero gradient, so gradient descent cannot
  train it. Use a smooth activation (ReLU/sigmoid/tanh) in trainable networks.

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Is a neuron just logistic regression?"** — A *single* sigmoid neuron is exactly logistic
regression. The difference is what you do next: stack neurons into hidden layers and the network
learns its own intermediate features, which a lone logistic-regression model cannot.

**"Why ReLU instead of sigmoid these days?"** — In deep networks, sigmoid and tanh *saturate*:
far from 0 their slope is almost zero, so gradients shrink toward nothing as they pass back
through many layers (the vanishing-gradient problem, L17). ReLU keeps a constant slope of 1 for
positive inputs, trains faster, and is cheap to compute — so it is the default hidden activation.

**"How many layers and neurons do I need?"** — More neurons mean more capacity and more risk of
overfitting (L09). There is no formula; you tune it like any other hyperparameter. L15 (capacity)
and L17 (regularization for deep nets) take this up — for now, one hidden layer is enough to beat
XOR.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---|---|
| Artificial neuron | a weighted sum $z = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x}+b$, then an activation $a=\phi(z)$ |
| Perceptron vs neuron | the perceptron is a neuron with $\phi$ fixed to a hard step |
| Activation function | the nonlinearity $\phi$; step / sigmoid / tanh / **ReLU** (modern default) |
| Why smooth $\phi$ | the step has zero gradient — useless for gradient descent (L03) |
| Dense layer | every input wired to every neuron: $\phi(\mathbf{X}\mathbf{W}+\mathbf{b})$ |
| XOR wall | not linearly separable, so one neuron fails (0.500) |
| Hidden layer | acts on what the previous layer computed, so it solves XOR (1.000) |
| Nonlinearity is key | stacked *linear* layers collapse to one linear map |
| MLP (next) | input to hidden layer(s) to output; the weights are *learned* (L15/L16) |
